blog_posts.dek: A step-by-step walkthrough of vetting licensure, scoping your project, and agreeing payment terms directly — without a single in-person meeting.
blog_posts.excerpt: A step-by-step walkthrough of vetting licensure, scoping your project, and agreeing payment terms directly — without a single in-person meeting.

blog_blocks.text: "It depends" is not a starting point. A good platform gives you an itemized typical range from square footage, add-ons, and a jurisdiction complexity score before you talk to anyone. Use it as your baseline — then each architect sets their own price, fixed or hourly, on the scoping call.

You hire and pay your architect directly, so settle terms in writing before drawings begin: a deposit, then payments tied to milestones you approve — schematic, design development, permit set. Avoid any arrangement that asks for the full fee up front, before you've seen a thing.
The best remote projects feel boring — clear scope, a real number, milestones you sign off before the next payment. Boring is what gets you a clean permit.

Once drawings are underway, everything should live in one place: files, comments, milestone sign-offs, and the submission itself. A tracked timeline keeps revision cycles short and gives your contractor a set they recognize — which is what clears plan check the first time.

case_studies.match_narrative: The estimate engine returned a typical price range from square footage, add-ons, and Oakland’s jurisdiction complexity score — a realistic baseline, not a quote. Within 48 hours the homeowner was reviewing two CA-licensed architects with hillside ADU experience, and hired one of them directly.

case_studies.quote: The estimate landed right in the range our architect quoted. She was licensed right here in Oakland, and the permit set cleared first try — no revisions.
